strengths: Addresses genuine practical problem: gradient-based data valuation is computationally prohibitive for billion-parameter models, and this work provides a practical solution with orders-of-magnitude efficiency improvements (seconds vs. hours)

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: diverse tasks (6 task types), architectures (Qwen, Llama), modalities (LLMs, VLMs), and model scales (1.5B-72B) with consistent high performance and proper baseline comparisons
Solid theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 rigorously connects learning dynamics to the proposed scoring formula, with clear mathematical decomposition and sound proof structure
Impressive empirical results: near-perfect or perfect AUC/Recall on multiple tasks; significant improvements on mislabeled detection (11.5% AUC gain on Qwen-VL-3B); stable across model scales

Practical algorithm design: Algorithm 1 is concrete and implementable; batching strategy and in-batch vocabulary optimization show engineering maturity; qualitative examples (Fig. 3) provide interpretable validation
Clear presentation: well-motivated problem statement, logical flow from theory to practice, detailed appendix with complete proofs and experimental details
weaknesses: Strong assumptions lack empirical validation: Assumption 1 (unconstrained features) is cited from neural collapse literature but never verified for tested LLMs/VLMs; Assumption 2 (distinct inputs) is critical for theory but no robustness analysis when violated

Gap between theory and practice: reduction from Eq. (1) to Eq. (2) lacks transparent justification; practical optimizations (in-batch vocabulary restriction) are theoretically unjustified and could introduce unquantified approximation errors

Incomplete ablation studies: α's importance shown qualitatively but no systematic sensitivity analysis; missing ablations on vocabulary restriction, embedding dimension sensitivity, and aggregation strategies across multiple validation samples

Experimental concerns: baseline checkpoints selected for highest AUC while single For-Value model used (cherry-picking bias); class-based pseudo-label evaluation is somewhat artificial; style generation notably underperforms (AUC 0.895) without explanation

Limited task diversity: all evaluated tasks have clear class structures (10 classes, 90-900 samples); no open-ended generation, long-horizon reasoning, or cross-domain tasks; dataset sizes small compared to realistic scenarios

Missing baselines: no comparison to simpler alternatives (pure cosine similarity, confidence-based selection); Emb baseline adapted from image generation rather than being a vanilla embedding similarity baseline

Theoretical-practical gap in scoring definition: Definition 1 specifies per-sample influence on single validation point, but practice aggregates across validation samples without principled justification for aggregation strategy

Reproducibility and scalability questions: no code availability mentioned; limited exploration of scaling to realistic training set sizes (10k-100k samples); checkpoint selection methodology for baselines lacks proper held-out validation set

strengths: Significant computational efficiency gains (seconds vs. hours), enabling data valuation for models up to 72B parameters
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple model sizes, types (LLM/VLM), and diverse tasks
Consistent strong empirical results with near-perfect AUC/Recall scores on most benchmarks
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and thorough supplementary material
Practical algorithm with implementation optimizations (in-batch vocabulary restriction) that reduce complexity from O(nd|V|) to O(nd|V̂|)
weaknesses: Weak theoretical foundation: Assumption 1 (unconstrained features) contradicts how neural networks work and lacks rigorous justification; Assumption 2 (distinct inputs) is acknowledged as strong but insufficiently analyzed
Theory-practice disconnect: Theorem 1 characterizes continuous-time learning dynamics (d/dt), but practice applies Eq. (1) at a single checkpoint without temporal integration or selection criterion
Questionable experimental setup: Toy datasets (900 training samples for LLM, 600 for VLM), unrealistic class-based pseudo-labels as ground truth, artificial 50% label noise for mislabeling detection
Suspiciously perfect results (AUC≈1.0 on most tasks) suggest evaluation may be too simple or method overfitting to the setup; style generation underperformance (AUC≈0.895) lacks analysis
Unfair baseline comparison: Baselines evaluated at best checkpoint post-hoc while For-Value requires only one forward pass; not apples-to-apples for computational claims
Limited novelty: Core contribution is essentially representation similarity + prediction error weighting; marginal improvement over Emb baseline is primarily the α term
No failure analysis: Missing discussion of when/why method fails, edge cases, or conditions limiting applicability
Unaddressed practical concerns: Memory requirements for storing representations (d×n), sensitivity to batch composition, impact of fine-tuning on frozen representations
Missing large-scale evaluation: No experiments on realistic datasets (millions of samples); behavior at scale remains unclear
Weak ground truth for influence: Class labels don't validate that identified samples actually improve model performance; no direct downstream task evaluation

strengths: Strong practical contribution: achieves data valuation in seconds vs. hours, enabling application to 72B parameter models where baselines are infeasible
Sound theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 is rigorously derived, showing influence arises from representation alignment and prediction error similarity, with proper decomposition of learning dynamics

Comprehensive experimental design: multiple diverse tasks (sentence transformations, math problems, VLM captioning), systematic model size evaluation (1.5B-72B), proper reporting of standard deviations, and effective qualitative examples
Consistent empirical improvements: For-Value matches or exceeds all baselines across LLM and VLM tasks while being orders of magnitude faster
Clear implementation and optimization: Algorithm 1 is explicit, and vocabulary-focused optimization (O(|V_D|d)) is well-motivated with minimal accuracy loss
Strong ablation demonstrating necessity of prediction error weighting: α term shows significant importance, with large gaps when set to 1
weaknesses: Critical unvalidated assumption: Assumption 1 (unconstrained features) is foundational to the theory but never empirically validated across models/architectures—no analysis of whether pretrained models actually satisfy this assumption

Uncharacterized theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 provides no approximation bounds; contribution of discarded Term II (token unembedding) is not quantified; violation of distinct input assumption is not analyzed

Limited real-world experimental validation: (1) Tasks are synthetic/simple (10 transformation templates); (2) Datasets are small (900 LLM, 30-800 VLM samples) vs. typical fine-tuning scale; (3) 50% mislabeling is unrealistic compared to 1-5% real-world noise; (4) AUC uses pseudo-labels (same class = 1) rather than ground-truth influence measured by train/test performance deltas

Incomplete ablation studies: Only one ablation tested (α=1); missing ablations on layer choice, batch size sensitivity, vocabulary size effects, and comparisons with simpler baselines (random sampling, perplexity ranking)

Suspicious experimental results: Perfect/near-perfect AUC scores (1.000 ± 0.001) suggest tasks may be too easy; style generation task dramatically underperforms (0.5-0.6 AUC) without clear explanation

Scope limitations inadequately discussed: (1) Method only applies to frozen pretrained models fine-tuned on downstream tasks—not full training or domain-adaptive pretraining; (2) Limited to autoregressive models with no discussion of encoder-only architectures; (3) No failure mode analysis
Computational complexity incomplete: O(MN) forward passes required; Table 3 ignores memory access patterns and I/O costs; per-sample valuation becomes expensive with millions of training examples

Weak baseline selection: Emb baseline (Yang et al. 2025) designed for generative image models, not autoregressive LLMs; missing comparisons with other training-free or simpler alternatives; TracIn and Wang et al. (2024) not empirically compared
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned; task-specific hyperparameters (LoRA settings) lack sensitivity analysis
Presentation issues: Inconsistent notation (z vs y), potentially confusing 'unconstrained features' terminology, unclear distinction between Theorem 1 and Equation (2) implementation

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: data valuation for billion-parameter models with significant computational constraints
Rigorous theoretical foundation with Theorem 1 providing closed-form data influence based on forward quantities; proofs are detailed and appear correct
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama, Qwen; 1.5B-72B), modalities (LLM, VLM), and tasks (influential data, mislabeled data, data selection)
Substantial efficiency improvements: 5-6x faster than HyperINF with execution times reduced from hours to minutes/seconds
Consistent strong empirical performance: achieves perfect or near-perfect AUC on multiple tasks; outperforms gradient-based baselines while using only forward passes
Clear presentation of methodology with detailed algorithm, ablation studies showing importance of prediction error term, and qualitative examples demonstrating meaningful influence capture
Reproducibility-focused: comprehensive experimental details, hyperparameters specified, code availability promised
weaknesses: Critical unvalidated assumptions: Unconstrained Features (Assumption 1) and Distinct Input (Assumption 2) are assumed but never empirically validated against the tested models. No analysis of whether hidden representations are actually unconstrained in practice

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 only applies at pretrained initialization (t=0), but practical applicability during/after training is unexplored. The method provides static influence scores only, limiting utility for dynamic data selection and active learning

Unfair baseline comparisons: For-Value measures influence from pretrained models while baselines fine-tune first, making them measure fundamentally different quantities ('initialization influence' vs. 'post-training influence'). This critical distinction is understated

Suspicious near-perfect results: Multiple instances of 1.0±0.001 or 1.0±0.000 AUC (Tables 1-2) raise credibility concerns. While footnote 2 attributes this to polarized distributions, deeper investigation is needed to rule out metric ceiling effects

Missing failure analysis: No systematic study of when/why For-Value fails or succeeds; limited investigation of what types of influence it captures well. Inconsistent results across tasks (0.895 AUC on style generation vs. 0.994 on subject generation) unexplained
Sparse vocabulary approximation is ad-hoc: Restricting computation to in-batch vocabulary lacks analysis of information loss; out-of-batch tokens may be semantically important

Limited scope inadequately discussed upfront: Method only applies to finetuning initialization, not pretraining or training dynamics. This substantial limitation is relegated to brief limitations section rather than highlighted in introduction

Experimental methodology concerns: (1) Baseline checkpoint selection by highest test AUC could bias results; (2) Pseudo-label evaluation using class overlap is indirect; (3) Data selection improvements often modest (48.3% vs 42.8% on GSM8K); (4) High variance on some metrics (Emb: 0.841±0.189 in Table 2)

strengths: Significant computational improvements (5-6× speedup) enabling practical scalability to 72B models, addressing a real bottleneck in existing methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks (influential data identification, mislabeled data detection, data selection) and model scales (1.5B-72B parameters)
Consistent performance relative to gradient-based baselines across diverse tasks, with meaningful ablation studies showing the importance of prediction error weighting
Algorithm 1 is efficiently implementable with sparse matrix operations, and the method naturally enables batch parallelization
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 applies only at t=0 (pretrained initialization), yet experiments measure performance after finetuning. No theoretical justification for why alignment at initialization predicts post-training behavior
Warm-up training used in practice (Section A.3) contradicts theoretical setup requiring t=0. This fundamental inconsistency undermines the theoretical motivation
Suspiciously perfect results across diverse tasks (Tables 1-2: AUC=1.0±0.001, Recall=1.0±0.001) suggest evaluation protocol issues. Class-overlap pseudo-labels are crude proxies for true influence
Data selection paradox: Table 3 shows 5% selection outperforming 100% full training (48.3% vs 47.8%), indicating potential overfitting or flawed evaluation protocol
Limited conceptual novelty: For-Value is essentially Emb baseline plus prediction error weighting. The structural similarity to embedding similarity methods is not adequately discussed

Methodological issues: Unfair baseline comparison (baselines use LoRA-adapted models while For-Value uses pretrained), no significance testing on marginal improvements (0.6-2% in Tables 4-5), checkpoint selection bias
Marginal practical improvements in data selection tasks (Tables 4-5) lack statistical validation and fall within typical noise margins despite computational expense
Dropped term (II) in derivation justified by Assumption 2, but no empirical analysis of term magnitude or validation that assumption holds for related training/validation data

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution with rigorous derivation of closed-form data value expression (Theorem 1) based on last-layer hidden representations and prediction errors
Significant practical efficiency gains: 5-6× speedup over state-of-the-art methods (HyperINF, DataInf) while maintaining comparable or superior effectiveness

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple dimensions: diverse task types (influential data identification, mislabeled detection, data selection), both LLMs and VLMs, model sizes from 1.5B to 72B parameters, and multiple domains (mathematics, medicine, vision-language)
Consistent high performance across benchmarks with near-perfect AUC/Recall scores and qualitatively sensible example rankings (Figure 5)
Enables batch parallelization naturally, addressing a critical limitation of gradient-based methods that require per-sample backpropagation
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem, transparent methodology, proper ablation studies demonstrating importance of prediction error term (α), and thorough appendix
weaknesses: Critical theoretical assumptions lack empirical validation: Unconstrained Features Assumption (Assumption 1) claims embeddings are independent of architectural complexities (LoRA, layer norm, attention), but this is not validated on tested models

No approximation error analysis: Theorem 1 shows what increases data value but provides no error bounds or analysis of when/why the approximation works; no comparison of last-layer gradient vs. full-layer influence

Limited scope: Method restricted to fine-tuning only; evaluates data value at initialization (t=0) which may not correlate with final performance; cannot support dynamic data selection during training
Incomplete analysis of key components: Impact of sample-associated vocabulary size |V̂| on complexity not thoroughly analyzed; limited investigation of failure modes or when method underperforms

Experimental design concerns: Synthetic mislabeling (50% random corruption) may not reflect real-world label noise; some data selection improvements are modest (Table 5: 52.23% vs 52.36%); high variance in results due to polarized value distributions

Missing practical details: Sensitivity to batch size and vocabulary composition not explored; performance under distribution shift not evaluated; typical |V̂| values and scaling behavior not documented
Distinct Input Assumption (Assumption 2) extension to overlapping outputs mentioned but not empirically validated; different hardware/quantization settings make baseline comparisons somewhat unequal
